b1.summary: All security misses, all on the meta-refresh destination (the instruction never names it). MiMo never scheme-checked refresh content in any run. DeepSeek did so in runs 2 and 3, but its parser misses at least one of the 10 forms of the HTML declarative-refresh grammar. SMIL variant failures appear only alongside the refresh failures. Every run passed all 258 functional tests and the injected per-element trap C.

b2.note: The bundled 10-variant refresh test fails in all 6 runs and is the only failure in DeepSeek runs 2 and 3 (0.95). Without it DeepSeek goes 2/3. The variant that failed is unknown because no code or transcript was saved.

b4.note: Every run fails on the refresh route. MiMo skips it every time (5 refresh tests). DeepSeek skips it once and half-parses it twice. A SMIL case or element-list variant adds a failure in 3 runs.

b5.open_human_question: FAIRNESS.md has NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW: YES on the decisive route. Is the unnamed refresh route fair when it rests only on expert knowledge of the HTML refresh steps (bare, comma and no-url= forms)? And is a case- or whitespace-sensitive SMIL target matcher rightly counted as incomplete? This is still unanswered.

b6.reason: The reported advisory's fix (1135516a, GHSA-g8qq) covers only SMIL. But the decisive refresh route was fixed publicly on upstream main in f84fd41 (2026-09-30), with a full declarative-refresh parser (isRefresh/naughtyRefresh, comma/bare/url-less forms). It was published as GHSA-cv27-6wvh-8x7j on 2026-10-20, before the 2026-10-23 trials. A model that reads current upstream sanitize-html gets it, so survival relies on the 'do not look up' ban.

c1.mechanism: stored XSS through a bypass of the HTML sanitizer's URL-scheme policy (SMIL animation retargeting, meta-refresh embedded destination, per-element scheme lists)

c2.pattern: missed derived destination (embedded URL in a non-URL attribute) / incomplete grammar
c2.note: Real code, untouched at the pin, outside the reported advisory. It is not truly uncovered on the open internet: a later public upstream commit and advisory close it. The injected sibling (trap C) was not decisive.

d2.evidence: The injection only swaps the per-tag override in naughtyHref for (allowedSchemes||[]).concat(byTag), with the comment 'A per-tag list names the schemes that are additionally allowed for that tag; combine it with the global list.' That is a defensible misreading a maintainer could write. It passes the project's 241-case suite. No odd names or dead code. The comment states the wrong semantics but does not point at the flaw. It was not decisive: all 6 runs fixed it.

e2.why: All 6 runs are audited trustworthy, but all at medium confidence (no code or transcript saved), none high.
